To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a single inoculation of mice with an adenoviral vector expressing HSV glyco-protein B induces protective immunity against a lethal challenge with the homologous virus.
mice inoculated with a recombinant human adenovirus expressing HSV glycoproteins B were protected from lethal challenge with HSV.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an adenovirus vaccine for HSV.
the use of recom binant human adenovirus as a vaccine vector for HSV.
the use of recombi- nant adenoviruses expressing gB as vaccines against herpes simplex virus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of human adenovirus vectors for vaccination against HSV appears to be a promising and safe method of inducing immunity.
the use of adenoviruses expressing gB is a promising approach to the development of an effective vaccine against HSV.
the use of adenovirus vector as a vaccine is a very promising approach to induce a strong immune response and protect mice against lethal challenge by HSV.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that a human adenovirus vector which expresses a foreign protein can be used as a vaccine to protect mice against lethal challenge by HSV.
a single oral inoculation of mice with AdgB 2 induces high titer antibodies to HSV gB which protect against lethal challenge with HSV.
a single inoculation of a recombinant human adenovirus vector can induce a high level of protection against a lethal challenge with a heterologous virus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the human adenovirus vector AdgB2 induces high levels of gB in mice and that this gB can protect mice against lethal challenge.
recombinant adenoviuses expressing foreign genes can induce high titer antibody and cellular immune responses and can protect mice from a lethal challenge of HSV.
